overview: Praa Sands (pronounced 'pray') is about a mile of fine, shell-based sand on Cornwall's south coast, just off the A394 between Penzance and Helston. It faces south into Mount's Bay, sits inside the Cornwall National Landscape, and is backed by grass-topped dunes with headlands at each end. Because it faces the opposite way to the north coast, it's the beach many surfers head for when northerly winds have blown the north-coast breaks out.

Most people arrive at the western end, where the car parks, a café, a general store and a slipway give an easy, level route onto the sand. Walk east towards Hendra and it gets noticeably quieter. Erosion has exposed a thin layer of peat around 2,000 years old that was once buried under the dunes, which is why the beach is listed as a regionally important geological site. A wartime pillbox has slipped from the cliff onto the sand.

There's history behind the beach too. A memorial on the green remembers the damaged Sunderland flying boat beached here in 1943, when villagers helped its crew ashore. The South West Coast Path runs along the back of the beach, east to Rinsey Head and west towards Marazion and St Michael's Mount, so it's easy to mix a surf with a walk. Basking sharks, seals and dolphins are occasionally seen offshore.

text: Praa faces south, so it needs swell that makes its way into Mount's Bay, which gives it a different swell window from the north coast. When it does get swell, the waves can be powerful and are a test even for experienced surfers. It's often at its best around high tide, but that's also when the beach shelves fastest and the shorebreak can dump hard.

Light northerly winds are the ones to look for. The wind here can be very local and gusty, so it may be blowing at Praa when it's calm a few miles away. There are rocks near both headlands and the beach is known for strong undercurrents, so stay between the flags when lifeguards are on duty.

cards.label: Level
cards.title: Small days for learners
cards.text: Lessons run on suitable days; bigger swells bring powerful waves best left to experienced surfers.

cards.label: Wind
cards.title: Light northerly
cards.text: Offshore here, and often the reason to come when the north coast is messy.

cards.label: Hazards
cards.title: High-tide shorebreak
cards.text: Steeply shelving sand, a heavy shore dump at high tide, undercurrents and rocks by the headlands.

practical.label: Parking
practical.title: Western end car parks
practical.text: The car parks are at the western end, with a level route to the sand via the slipway. The eastern end at Hendra is a longer walk.

practical.label: Facilities
practical.title: Clustered at the western end
practical.text: Toilets are near the car parks and beach entrance, with a café overlooking the sand, a general store and a surf shop nearby.

practical.label: Lifeguards
practical.title: Seasonal RNLI patrol
practical.text: The RNLI patrols the main beach in season. No flags means no lifeguards; check this year's dates on the RNLI website.

practical.label: Dogs
practical.title: Peak-summer daytime ban
practical.text: Cornwall Council prohibits dogs on Praa Sands from 10am to 6pm, 1 July to 31 August. They're welcome at other times.

practical.label: Getting there
practical.title: A394
practical.text: About ten minutes' drive from Penzance towards Helston on the A394. Penzance is the nearest main railway station.

faqs.q: How do you pronounce Praa Sands?
When can dogs go on Praa Sands?
faqs.a: All year except 10am to 6pm from 1 July to 31 August.

faqs.q: Is Praa Sands good when the north coast is flat?
faqs.a: Not necessarily. Praa needs swell to reach Mount's Bay, so it's at its best when there's swell about but northerly winds have spoiled the north coast.

faqs.q: Is it safe to swim at high tide?
faqs.a: Take care. The sand shelves quickly at high tide and the shorebreak can be heavy, which is a particular risk for inexperienced swimmers. Swim between the red and yellow flags when lifeguards are on duty.
